rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its strongest line, "Monzo returns to the US — this time renting a banking license instead of chasing one," turns the update into a real regulation-market-access story and then names the missing proof. B has good bones, but "Monzo re-enters a US challenger-bank market that already has three incumbents" invents the competitive frame out of thin air. That is how a decent angle set walks itself into a correction.
gaps_in_A: "Monzo posted its first annual profit — then spent it on a second shot at America" overstates the causal link. The facts support timing, not that Monzo spent profit on the US push.
"renting a banking license" is punchy, but loose. The supplied fact is a partner-bank arrangement; the exact license mechanics need proof before that wording survives.
"home playbook" needs product detail. The update only gives checking accounts and budgeting tools, so this angle still needs concrete UK-vs-US comparison before pitching.
gaps_in_B: "Monzo re-enters a US challenger-bank market that already has three incumbents" is invented from the supplied facts. The update gives no incumbent count and no competitor landscape.
"Chime, Varo, Current" are not in the update. Naming them may be plausible market context, but this exercise asked for grounded angles, not memory cosplay.
"The prevailing assumption ... is that a neobank needs its own national charter to operate here" is an overbroad invented premise. The facts only say Monzo failed to secure one before.
"Monzo is explicitly pairing its first-ever annual profit with a second US run" says more than the update says. Same window, yes. Explicit pairing, no.
